transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Recording: fireflies-auto
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Miguel (Redwood Eng), Priya (HorizonHealth Head of ML), Ethan (Infra), Lina (SRE), Kumar (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood and HorizonHealth dug into KV cache behavior under long-context and heavy prefix-reuse workloads. Discussed eviction patterns (LRU-like), paging to system memory, observed tail-latency spikes at ~8-12k tokens when multiple concurrent sessions share cache entries. Action: Redwood to share KV cache trace and eviction logs; HorizonHealth to run benchmark.

Topics: KV cache eviction, paging (GPU->CPU), long-context workloads, prefix reuse strategies, quantization effects on cache entries, batching interactions, on-prem/VPC tuning

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya: Priya here. Ethan here. Lina here. Kumar on audio.
[00:18] Jordan: Great. Samira, Miguel, you with us?
[00:22] Samira: Yep Samira on deck. Miguel's on as well.
[00:26] Jordan: Thanks. We'll jump straight into the KV cache stuff — you sent an example of the long prefix workload, Priya, right?
[00:32] Priya: Yeah we put up a long clinical note generation scenario — like 12k tokens per session, lots of shared prefixes for templates. We started seeing weird latency regressions after about 6 to 8k tokens.

[00:48] Samira: Okay that's consistent with a caching edge case we've seen — when prefix reuse is high and the KV rows are large, eviction and paging interplay can cause tail latency. Before we go deep, quick config check — are you on Dedicated or Private?
[01:05] Ethan: We're on Redwood Private in our colo, 4x A40s for inference, and we use your containerized runtime. We're seeing GPU memory pressure climb and then some requests get paged to CPU and latency jumps.

[01:22] Miguel: A40s, got it. We need to clarify: when you say 'paged to CPU' do you mean the runtime is moving KV cache pages to host memory, or is it offloading kv-shards to disk?
[01:33] Lina: Host memory, mostly — we saw high host-mem usage. Swap wasn't heavily used but there was a blip.

[01:40] Samira: That points to our soft-eviction path where we try to keep large KV entries in GPU but degrade to host if memory pressure crosses threshold. Eviction policy by default is an LRU-ish policy with segment weighting — new large prefixes can push out older, frequently reused smaller prefixes.

[02:02] Priya: LRU-ish? Can you explain segment weighting? We rely on prefix reuse across patients; losing a prefix that is reused hurts throughput a lot.

[02:14] Samira: Sure — our current policy tracks recency plus an estimated per-entry token cost. So a 4k-token prefix consumes more weight than a 64-token one. The eviction score is recency_score / token_cost-ish, we know it's a simplification. That means big prefixes can get evicted if they are older even if used somewhat frequently.

[02:41] Kumar: That seems bad for our templates which are long and reused many times a day. Is there a knob to prefer prefix reuse frequency over size?

[02:52] Miguel: We do have a config flag — cache.reuse_bias or something — that increases frequency weight. But on Private we often leave defaults. We should share exact flag names after the call.

[03:05] Samira: Right, cache.max_entries and cache.reuse_bias are tunables. For long templates we recommend bumping cache.max_entries and enabling reuse_bias to favor frequency. But you will need enough GPU memory; otherwise you'll hit our paging fallback.

[03:22] Ethan: When paging occurs, what's the observed perf delta? We saw jumps from 30–40ms per token to 200–400ms on tails.

[03:33] Samira: Those numbers line up with differences between GPU-local KV hits and host-memory access + memcpy. Paging can add 5–10x latency per token depending on memcpy sizes. Also concurrency matters: one big page move can block other streams in our current runtime iteration.

[03:54] Priya: Is that blocking an implementation detail — can we reduce blocking?

[03:59] Miguel: We're working on async page transfers and finer-grained locking; some customers on latest private builds get better overlap. But on your current image, we still serialize some operations.

[04:16] Lina: We noticed that sometimes eviction happens even when GPU memory shows 10% free. Could there be fragmentation?

[04:24] Samira: Yes fragmentation is nontrivial — the runtime chops KV store into variable-sized slabs. If there's no contiguous block large enough for an incoming prefix, we may evict and compact which can temporarily show free memory but not usable.

[04:44] Jordan: Quick diagram note — fragmentation + large-entry allocations -> compaction pauses -> apparent free memory but inability to allocate contiguous slab -> eviction.

[04:58] Ethan: Any suggestions for immediate mitigations?

[05:03] Samira: Short term: 1) Increase cache.max_entries; 2) Enable reuse_bias; 3) Increase gpu alloc slab size (gpu.kv_slab_min) so large prefixes fit without fragmentation. Also tune batch sizes to reduce concurrent per-GPU memory pressure.

[05:26] Priya: For the second item, reuse_bias, what is the recommended value?

[05:30] Samira: Start with 0.6 (range 0.0–1.0) — 0.6 biases frequency moderately. We can provide a tuned advisory for your workload after you share traces.

[05:42] Kumar: Would quantization affect KV size? We're using int8 offline models.

[05:47] Miguel: Good point — quantization reduces model weights but the KV cache is activations-based; activation sizes per token are roughly proportional to hidden size and precision. If you use int8 activation packing we can drop per-token KV footprint by about 20–30% but correctness needs validating. Our quantized runtime currently uses 8-bit attention tensors but some customers prefer float16 for stability.

[06:13] Priya: We did a quantized run and saw marginally lower memory pressure but got occasional quality drift. So we held off. Does Redwood have safe defaults?

[06:22] Samira: Default is float16 activations; quantized paths are opt-in. We'll share notes on expected KV savings and gotchas.

[06:31] Ethan: Back to eviction — you mentioned honoring frequency over size. Are there heuristics for eviction granularity? We see the runtime evicting whole prefixes rather than partial pages.

[06:44] Samira: Currently eviction is per-key (prefix). We could do partial eviction by splitting very large prefix entries into chunked subkeys — that's on the roadmap but not in your current build. Chunking would allow keeping hot prefix heads while evicting tail tokens.

[07:03] Priya: Chunking sounds promising. Any interim workaround? Partitioning templates into smaller prefixes?

[07:10] Miguel: Yes you can restructure prompts to have a stable small prefix followed by variable suffix that is generated. That increases effective reuse of the small cached portion. But I know that's not always possible with your templates.

[07:22] Priya: Our templates often include patient-specific context embedded early, so splitting isn't straightforward.

[07:28] Lina: Could we do a hybrid cache: keep a persistent cache for shared templates and a transient per-session cache for patient data?

[07:36] Samira: The runtime supports namespaced caches — public/shared vs session-local. If you can mark the templates as shared keys and keep patient context session-only, the shared keys survive eviction more easily. But requires instrumentation from client side.

[07:50] Jordan: Quick pause — I'm going to drop a link to an internal doc and a sample trace in the chat; please look for those after this call.

[08:00] Jordan: (link) https://redwood.example/docs/kvcache-tuning (note: placeholder)

[08:10] Ethan: Thanks. On the trace you asked for, what exactly do you need instrumented?

[08:15] Samira: Ideally: per-request KV hit/miss, per-key size, eviction events with timestamps, GPU mem usage per second, mem fragmentation snapshots, and any memcpy/page events. The trace format we use is simple JSON line entries — I'll send a sample.

[08:34] Priya: Perfect. We can add that to our staging run.

[08:38] Kumar: A question on page thresholds — what triggers migration to host memory?

[08:44] Miguel: There are two thresholds: a soft threshold that triggers background migration once GPU free falls below soft_limit (default 15%), and a hard threshold that forces immediate eviction when below hard_limit (default 4%). The background migration tries to move least-recently-used large entries to host proactively.

[09:04] Lina: Are those values configurable in Private runtime?

[09:08] Samira: Yes, gpu.kv_soft_limit and gpu.kv_hard_limit are tunables. On your workload I'd set soft_limit to 25% to give more headroom and avoid urgent migration.

[09:21] Priya: Will raising soft_limit increase host memory usage a lot?

[09:25] Samira: It will increase host-mapped KV presence but reduces hard thrashing. It's a trade-off — more host memory vs lower tail latency.

[09:34] Ethan: We have 512GB host mem per node so that's ok. Concern is memcpy rate.

[09:40] Miguel: If host mem is abundant, we can tune migration to be more aggressive asynchronously so memcpy bandwidth is used during low-util windows.

[09:50] Jordan: Another pattern we've seen — when multiple streams share the same large prefix and one stream triggers migration, others get penalized during the memcpy window. We need to consider per-key locks to avoid global stalls.

[10:05] Samira: We're prototyping per-key soft locks so a memcpy for KeyA only blocks readers of KeyA; currently coarse locks sometimes cause all streams to wait.

[10:15] Priya: Any estimate on when per-key locking ship?

[10:19] Miguel: For Private customers we can backport a patch; ETA a couple weeks with QA. Will confirm in follow-up.

[10:28] Priya: Great. One more — what about batching interactions? We use dynamic batching to maximize throughput; does batching increase KV pressure?

[10:38] Samira: Batching increases simultaneous active KV usage because multiple requests' KV lookups allocate in-flight buffers. If you increase batch size you may see higher peak memory. But batching reduces per-token compute cost; it's balancing act.

[10:50] Ethan: So for our 4x A40s we should limit in-flight batch to prevent peaks — recommended starting point?

[10:56] Samira: Start with batch_max 8 and measure. If your workload has long contexts, prefer smaller batch_max to throttle memory usage. We'll provide a guide.

[11:08] Kumar: Any monitoring signals you recommend for early warning?

[11:12] Samira: Track GPU free, fragmentation ratio (we emit frag_pct), eviction_rate_per_min, memcpy_bandwidth, and kv_hit_rate. Set alerts for frag_pct > 30% and eviction_rate spike.

[11:28] Priya: The frag_pct metric is new to us — can you point to the metric name?

[11:33] Samira: It's redwood.kv.fragmentation_pct in our exporter. Also redwood.kv.evictions and redwood.kv.mempcpy_bytes (typo — memcopy in exporter currently spelled memcpy, we'll fix).

[11:50] Jordan: Note on typos — open ticket for exporter metric name cleanup.

[11:55] (brief cross talk)
[12:05] Priya: We also saw a scenario where cold-starting many sessions caused a deluge of unique prefixes and eviction storms. Any technique to mitigate?

[12:16] Samira: Common technique: pre-warm shared prefixes into GPU cache at startup (a cache preload). We support a preload manifest that the runtime loads at boot. You can also seed some templates via API.

[12:28] Ethan: Preloading sounds useful. Does it persist across restarts?

[12:33] Miguel: Preload runs at startup; on restarts you can reapply the manifest. We have a persistent cache option on roadmap to checkpoint hot keys but not yet GA.

[12:46] Priya: If we preload does it count against memory limits?

[12:50] Samira: Yes, it consumes GPU memory like a normal cache entry. Preload should be balanced with soft_limit settings.

[13:00] Kumar: On the topic of long-context — are you seeing KV metadata blow up nonlinearly with context length? We expected linear growth but observed some superlinear behavior in our traces after 10k tokens.

[13:12] Samira: Superlinear could be due to duplicate stored keys with slight tokenization boundary differences — when user prompts vary slightly we store many near-duplicates. Tokenization determinism and consistent prefix normalization helps.

[13:28] Priya: We do some free-text fields added early; maybe those variations cause duplication.

[13:33] Samira: Consider canonicalizing variable fields or using placeholder tokens that expand at runtime rather than embedding raw text into cached prefixes.

[13:45] Ethan: We have a question around KV index size — what on-disk overhead to expect?

[13:50] Miguel: Index overhead is small relative to value sizes — approx 6–12% depending on metadata. The big cost is value payloads.

[14:00] Priya: Does the runtime evict based on index heuristics or purely value weight?

[14:05] Samira: Value weight is primary but we include index hotness as part of score. That's why sometimes small index entries persist even if value large — heuristics are complex.

[14:20] Priya: Any debug flags to force eviction logging?

[14:24] Samira: Yes set log.kv_eviction=debug and tracer.kv=1 in the runtime config, it'll emit event lines. We'll share an example.

[14:35] Jordan: (note) Sharing example logs after call.

[14:40] Priya: We also wanted to ask about cross-GPU routing — if a prefix is present on GPU0 but a request hits GPU2, do you fetch from remote GPU or recompute cache entry?

[14:52] Miguel: Two modes: replication and on-demand fetch. By default we replicate hot keys across GPUs up to a replication_budget. That reduces remote fetches but increases memory. On-demand remote fetch pulls from peer GPU via NVLink if available; else host relay.

[15:10] Priya: NVLink is present in our nodes. Is replication_budget tunable per-key?

[15:16] Samira: Not per-key yet — global policy. But you can mark keys as pinned/repl to force replication. Pinning is an API call.

[15:26] Ethan: Pinning API — good. That could help our shared templates be present across all GPUs.

[15:31] Kumar: Any caveats with pinned keys and eviction?

[15:35] Miguel: Pinned keys are excluded from normal eviction unless you explicitly unpin or low-level hard_limit forces reclamation. Use pin sparingly.

[15:50] Priya: Next — instrumentation for long-run tests. We'll do a 6-hour soak with variable prefixes. What metrics should we collect?

[15:58] Samira: At minimum: redwood.kv.fragmentation_pct, redwood.kv.evictions_total, redwood.kv.page_out_bytes, redwood.kv.page_in_bytes, redwood.kv.replication_events, host.mem.free, gpu.mem.free per GPU, per-request latency P50/P95/P99.

[16:18] Ethan: Will do. For the benchmark, what's a recommended concurrency pattern for us to stress both KV and batching?

[16:24] Samira: Use a mix: many sessions with long contexts (12k tokens) and high prefix reuse, plus a smaller set of ad-hoc sessions to force unique keys. Keep concurrency moderate (40–80) to simulate production; adjust batch_max accordingly.

[16:38] Priya: How about eviction debugging — can we replay eviction events to reproduce?

[16:44] Miguel: We'll provide a reproducible harness: a sequence of requests and a preload manifest plus an instrumentation script. Replaying is plausible.

[16:55] Jordan: Sounds like agreed next steps: Redwood provides traces, sample configs, and preload manifest; Horizon runs benchmarks and shares results.

[17:02] Priya: Quick question — are there any known issues when using our VPC NATs that affect peer fetches? We saw occasional timeouts.

[17:10] Samira: Peer fetches via host relay assume internal connectivity on certain ports; VPC egress/NAT misconfig can cause transient failures. We'll send a network checklist (ports, link-local addresses, MTU).

[17:26] Ethan: Please send that. We had an MTU mismatch once that slowed NVLink fallbacks.

[17:34] Kumar: Any recommendations on quantization + paging? Do they interact poorly?

[17:40] Miguel: Quantized activations may compress retrieved pages more compactly but memcpy patterns are similar. We recommend validating quality at target token lengths.

[17:50] Priya: Let's talk about an observed edge case — eviction storms during model rollouts when keys change shape. We saw a rollout cause immediate cache churn.

[17:59] Samira: Rollouts that change hidden size or KV layout will invalidate cache entries. Best practice: warm new model variants with preload and do gradual traffic ramp. Also keep model ABI stable when possible.

[18:15] Jordan: Can the runtime detect incompatible KV layouts and auto-fall back gracefully?

[18:20] Miguel: It can detect format mismatch and will be forced to rebuild cache; we emit a warning. Auto-fallback is limited — better to coordinate push.

[18:32] Priya: On the topic of rolling restarts, is there a way to checkpoint cache and restore?

[18:38] Samira: Not GA. We have experimental checkpointing for hot keys but it's not recommended for critical paths yet.

[18:48] Ethan: Oof. That would help our zero-downtime goals.

[18:52] Miguel: We're prioritizing it.

[19:00] Priya: A few quick clarifying questions from our infra team: 1) Does fragmentation metric count hole bytes only? 2) Are eviction events guaranteed to include key sizes?

[19:12] Samira: 1) frag_pct is hole_bytes / total_allocated_bytes. 2) eviction events include key id and value_size; if you enable tracer.kv we emit both.

[19:24] Priya: Good.

[19:30] (short pause, some background noise)
[19:45] Lina: We ran one test with heavy prefix reuse and saw steady-state KV hit rate ~94% but tail P99 still high, why?

[19:55] Samira: Because even with high hit rate, the small fraction of misses or mid-flight migrations can dominate P99. Also long-running sessions that touch very long tail tokens can incur serialization.

[20:10] Miguel: Consider adding localized retries and fast-fail strategies for cold misses — degrade to smaller model variant temporarily to keep latency SLOs.

[20:23] Priya: We have degrade-to-smaller-model logic in our stack; how quickly can Redwood route to smaller variant?

[20:30] Samira: Routing policy can be per-route; failover is immediate if the runtime marks a model unhealthy. There's a small cost to spin up a variant if not warm. Warmed variants are fast.

[20:42] Kumar: Any guidance for model warmers?

[20:45] Miguel: Keep a small pool of warmed containers with repinned keys so failover is instant. Warmers can be low-rps just to keep cache live.

[20:56] Priya: For our compliance audits, we need to record eviction events and who triggered them. Does Redwood audit evictions per-org?

[21:06] Samira: Yes our Private runtime can emit audit logs with event metadata. We can include user/session id in eviction logs if your client passes session metadata.

[21:18] Priya: We'll enable that.

[21:22] Jordan: Quick check: are there any more questions on tuning knobs before we move to the diagnostics plan?

[21:29] Ethan: I'm clear. Could you confirm the knob names in the doc? Sometimes names differ between versions.

[21:35] Samira: We'll send exact config keys and expected ranges in follow-up: cache.max_entries, cache.reuse_bias, gpu.kv_slab_min, gpu.kv_soft_limit, gpu.kv_hard_limit, batch.max, log.kv_eviction, tracer.kv, pin_key API.

[21:52] Priya: Thank you. For the diagnostic tracer — is there a size impact? Do traces blow up disk?

[21:58] Miguel: Traces can be verbose if you enable per-token logs. We recommend sampling or enabling full tracing for short windows. We'll provide a compact trace mode.

[22:12] Priya: That helps.

[22:18] (background typing)
[22:30] Jordan: Okay moving onto concrete reproduction steps. Samira, can you outline what we'll share?

[22:35] Samira: We'll share three artifacts: 1) a sample trace schema + small example log; 2) recommended runtime config + recommended starting values; 3) a preload manifest example and a small harness to replay the sequence.

[22:53] Priya: ETA for that?

[22:55] Samira: We'll upload within 48 hours.

[23:00] Ethan: We'll schedule the 6-hour soak to start 2025-02-14 and share results by 2025-02-18.

[23:10] Priya: One ask — can you include a minimal config that switches to chunked-prefix simulation so we can test partial eviction behavior?

[23:18] Miguel: We'll include a simulated chunking toggle in the harness. Not production-grade but useful for experimentation.

[23:28] Kumar: Cool. Anything else?

[23:32] Jordan: Quick recap and next steps out loud?

[23:35] Priya: Go ahead.

[23:36] Jordan: Redwood to deliver: KV trace example, config keys + explanations, preload manifest, chunking sim harness, network checklist. Horizon to run soak and benchmark, share perf sheet. Follow-up meeting week of 2025-02-20.

[23:55] Priya: Sounds good. We'll also include our tokenization stabilization changes as part of benchmark.

[24:02] Samira: Perfect. I'll also include notes on quantization tradeoffs we discussed.

[24:08] Ethan: Quick final: can you also include recommended alert thresholds in the doc?

[24:12] Samira: Yes we'll include suggested thresholds and Grafana queries.

[24:18] Jordan: Awesome. Any final comments?

[24:22] Kumar: Thanks everyone.

[24:24] Priya: Thanks — helpful discussion.

[24:28] (meeting closes; small chitchat)

[58:00] End recording

Notes and caveats: transcription contains some minor errors and shorthand (memcpy spelled as memcpy, exporter metric typos) that reflect in-call shorthand; links and configs will be delivered post-call.
